gap: No result ChatGPT got says why most built-in cables stop at 60 W. Under the USB-C cable rule, a cable without an electronic marker (e-marker) chip is rated at 3 A, and 3 A at 20 V is 60 W. A cable can carry more than 60 W only if it is rated above 3 A: UGREEN's 100 W retractable cable advertises 20 V/5 A (ChargerLAB), while ESR's Xtend tops out at 20 V/3 A.
standout_why: I compared this against the pages ChatGPT cited: UGREEN's retractable hub page, the UGREEN 100W product page, Belkin's 67W FAQ (337679) and The Verge's Baseus EnerCore piece. I also checked ChargerLAB's 100W teardown, which was in ChatGPT's results but not cited. UGREEN's hub page gives no cable watts or length at all. Belkin's FAQ gives '67W when charging one device' but no volts or amps and doesn't say whether that is the cable. ChargerLAB lists the 20V5A setting for the 100W cable but never says that 3 A (60 W) is the limit for a cable without a 5 A rating. ChatGPT called the UGREEN 65W cable's 60 W limit 'the notable trap' but never said what causes it. No page gives the 3 A / 5 A reason, which lets a shopper read any cable's volts × amps and tell whether it can go past 60 W.
decides: This confirms the pick and makes it easy to check. The 60 W limit comes from cable current, so a cable rated above 60 W has to advertise more than 3 A. The UGREEN Nexode 100W Retractable passes: ChargerLAB measured a 20V/5A setting and PPS up to 5 A on the cable itself, so it stays the top pick for full-power laptop charging through the cable. The ESR Xtend 45W (5–20 V, up to 3 A per ESR) and the UGREEN Nexode 65W Retractable (60 W cable) both hit the 3 A ceiling. They suit phones and small laptops, not 65 W+ laptops through the cable. A new lead from a partner store: the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W with Retractable USB-C Cable (us.ugreen.com, $149.99, read 2026-11-27). GeekDad and UGREEN-sourced coverage say its cable gives up to 140 W, which would beat the 100W model. 140 W over USB-C requires PD 3.1 at 28 V/5 A, but I could not open UGREEN's page to confirm the cable's volts and amps, so it should not displace the 100W pick until that figure is read. Also, our record has the UGREEN 100W at $42.49, but today's storecheck search of us.ugreen.com returned $49.99 (compare-at $59.99). Re-read the price before rendering.

findings.label: Current limit for a USB-C cable without an electronic marker
findings.value: Cables rated above 3 A must carry an electronic marker. A USB 2.0 Type-C cable 'may be electronically marked (required if cable supports >3A)'. At 20 V, 3 A = 60 W.
findings.source_title: Texas Instruments technical article SSZTBJ8 (Brian Gosselin and Nate Enos, May 2016)
findings.note: TI's summary of the USB Type-C spec, quoted verbatim: 'cables are required to be electronically marked if they are either full-featured and/or rated at more than 3A'. The article names 2 cable current ratings; the table that lists them is an image, so the 3 A and 5 A values come from the >3A wording. 60 W = 20 V × 3 A is my arithmetic. TI also defines a 'captive cable' (one end soldered in place or a non-USB connector), which is what a built-in retractable cable is. I could not confirm whether the e-marker requirement applies to captive cables, so the page should present the 3 A / 60 W ceiling as a current-rating limit, not as proof that a built-in cable has a chip.
